title: Stress, strain and Young's modulus
goals: Work out the stress in a bar, a tie or a pin from the load and the area
Work out strain from a stretch, or from a strain gauge reading, and turn it into stress
Work out how far a steel or aluminium part stretches under load
Read a stress–strain curve: elastic, yield, ultimate strength, fracture
Size a part from its yield strength and a factor of safety
summary:
**Stress** is load spread over area: $\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$. With F in newtons and A in mm², stress comes out in N/mm², which is the same as **MPa**. (1 MPa is also 10 bar.) Pulling is **tensile** stress, squashing **compressive**. A pin or bolt being cut sideways is in **shear**: $\tau = \frac{F}{A}$ over the area being cut; in a clevis the pin is in **double shear**, two areas.

The area of a round bar: $A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$.

**Strain** is the stretch as a fraction of the length: $\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}$. No units; often in **microstrain** (millionths). A strain gauge reads it directly.

**Young's modulus** is stiffness: $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$. Steel about **200 GPa** (200 000 N/mm²), aluminium about **70 GPa**, so aluminium stretches about three times as much under the same stress. Stiffness is not strength.

Put together: $\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AE}$, every length in mm and E in N/mm².

The **stress–strain curve**: a straight **elastic** part (it springs back), the **yield** point (it stays bent), the top, the **ultimate tensile strength** (UTS), then **fracture**. Ductile metals stretch a lot before breaking; brittle ones (cast iron, glass) hardly at all.

Design keeps stress well inside the elastic part: **allowable stress = yield strength ÷ factor of safety**. S275 structural steel yields at 275 MPa; with a factor of safety of 2.5, design to 110 MPa.

formulas.name: Stress
formulas.says: The load shared out over the area carrying it.
symbols: the stress (N/mm², the same as MPa)

formulas.name: Area of a round bar
formulas.says: The area of a circle from its diameter: π times the radius squared, written with the diameter.

formulas.name: Strain
formulas.says: How much it stretched, as a fraction of how long it was.

formulas.name: Young's modulus
formulas.says: The material's stiffness: how much stress it takes to make a given strain, in its elastic range.

formulas.name: Extension of a bar
formulas.says: Stress over stiffness gives the strain, and strain times length gives the stretch, all in one line.

formulas.name: Allowable stress
formulas.says: Keep the working stress the factor of safety below the stress at which the material starts to yield.
symbols: the factor of safety (a number, such as 2.5)
formulas.example: S275 with a factor of safety of 2.5: $\frac{275}{2.5} = 110$ MPa.

bench.task: Find the load rating on a lifting eye bolt, shackle or a fixing's data sheet, and check it from its size and material. Read only: no load testing.
check: Note the thread or pin diameter and the material grade
Work out the area: $\frac{\pi d^2}{4}$ (for a thread, the data sheet's tensile stress area is smaller)
Multiply by the yield strength to find the load at which it would start to yield
Divide by the marked working load: that ratio is roughly the factor of safety the maker used

cards.q: Two steel bars carry the same pull. One has twice the cross-section area of the other. The stress in the thicker bar is…
options: half that in the thinner bar
the same as in the thinner bar
twice that in the thinner bar
a quarter of that in the thinner bar
cards.why: Stress is load ÷ area. Twice the area shares the same load over twice the metal: half the stress. (A quarter is what you get for twice the diameter, because the area goes with the diameter squared.)

cards.title: Stress: load over area
cards.body:
**Stress** is how hard the material is being worked: the load shared out over the area carrying it.

$$\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$$

$\sigma$ (sigma) is the stress, $F$ the load in newtons, $A$ the area in mm². The answer is in **N/mm²**, the same as **MPa** (megapascals).

Pulling gives **tensile** stress; pushing, **compressive**. Strength figures for metals are given in MPa, so you compare like with like.
cards.more:
Stand on soft ground in trainers and you leave a print; in stilettos the heel sinks in. Same weight, much smaller area: more stress.

Numbers: a tie rod carries 10 kN (10 000 N). It is 100 mm² in section. Every square millimetre carries $10\,000 \div 100 = 100$ N: 100 N/mm², 100 MPa. Mild steel starts to yield at about 250–275 MPa, so this is comfortable.

1 MPa is also 10 bar: a hydraulic system at 200 bar is pressing on its walls at 20 MPa. Stress and pressure are the same kind of thing.

cards.q: A tie carries {kn} kN. Its cross-section is {ar} mm². What is the stress in it?
cards.why: Load in newtons (kN × 1000) over area in mm² gives N/mm², which is MPa.
cards.hint: kN × 1000 for newtons; ÷ area in mm².

cards.title: The area of a round bar
cards.body:
Most loaded parts are round: rods, pins, bolts. The area from the **diameter**:

$$A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$$

Double the diameter and the area goes up **four** times, so the stress for the same load falls to a quarter.

For a bolt, the thread cuts into the section: use the **tensile stress area** from the bolt tables (an M12 bolt is 84.3 mm², not the 113 mm² of a 12 mm bar).
cards.more:
The area of a circle is π times the radius squared. The radius is half the diameter, so $\pi \left(\frac{d}{2}\right)^2 = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$.

A 20 mm bar: $20^2 = 400$, $\times \pi = 1257$, $\div 4 = 314$ mm².

The usual slip is $\pi d^2$ without the 4, which makes the area four times too big and the stress four times too small: a part that looks safe and is not. A quick check: a 10 mm bar is about 79 mm², so a bit under 80.

cards.q: A round steel rod {dd} mm in diameter carries a pull of {kn} kN. What is the stress in it?
cards.why: Area first, from the diameter; then load over area. Forgetting the ÷ 4 makes the stress four times too low.
cards.hint: $A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$, then $\sigma = \frac{F}{A}$ with F in newtons.

cards.title: Strain and stiffness
cards.body:
Under load a part stretches a little. **Strain** is the stretch as a fraction of the length:

$$\varepsilon = \frac{\Delta L}{L}$$

$\varepsilon$ (epsilon) has no units; small strains are written in **microstrain** (millionths).

**Young's modulus** $E$ is how stiff the material is: stress per unit strain, $E = \frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}$. Steel is about **200 GPa** (200 000 N/mm²); aluminium about **70 GPa**. So under the same stress, aluminium stretches about three times as much as steel.
cards.more:
A 2 m steel bar that stretches 1 mm has a strain of $1 \div 2000 = 0.0005$: 500 microstrain.

Stiffness and strength are different things. An aluminium alloy can be as strong as mild steel (both yield around 250–300 MPa) but it is a third as stiff: a frame made of it bends three times as far under the same load unless the sections are made deeper.

A **strain gauge** is a fine foil grid glued to a part: it stretches with the part and its resistance changes, so the bridge circuit reads microstrain. Times E gives the stress in the part: 500 microstrain on steel is $0.0005 \times 200\,000 = 100$ MPa. That is how load cells work.

cards.q: A strain gauge on a steel beam (E = 200 000 N/mm²) reads {mu} microstrain. What is the stress there?
cards.why: Stress = modulus × strain, with microstrain × $10^{-6}$ as the strain. A shortcut for steel: every 5 microstrain is 1 MPa.

cards.q: A steel bar and an aluminium bar of the same size carry the same load. How does the aluminium bar's stretch compare?
options: It depends only on the load
cards.why: Same load and area means the same stress. Aluminium's E (about 70 GPa) is about a third of steel's (200 GPa), so it takes three times the strain. The stress is the same; the stretch is not.

cards.title: The stress–strain curve
cards.body:
Pull a mild steel test bar until it breaks and plot stress against strain:

- **Elastic**: a straight line; take the load off and it springs back. The slope is $E$.
- **Yield**: it starts to stretch for good: a **permanent set**. Mild steel: about 250–355 MPa.
- **Ultimate tensile strength** (UTS): the top of the curve, the most stress it takes.
- **Fracture**: it necks down and breaks.

**Ductile** metals stretch a long way after yielding (a warning before failure). **Brittle** ones, such as cast iron, break with almost no stretch.
cards.more:
Bend a paperclip a little and it springs back: elastic. Bend it more and it stays bent: past yield. Keep bending it back and forth and it snaps: fatigue, another lesson.

Designers work in the straight part, well below yield, so parts always spring back. The UTS matters for how much reserve there is and for things meant to break, like shear pins.

Ductility is a safety feature: a steel bracket that is overloaded bends visibly before it breaks, and someone notices. A cast iron one cracks without warning.

cards.q: Match each part of the stress–strain curve with what it means.
pairs: It springs back when the load comes off
The highest stress it can take
cards.why: Design keeps working stresses in the elastic region, well below yield.

cards.title: Factor of safety
cards.body:
Loads are not known exactly, materials vary, and parts wear. So a design keeps the working stress well below yield:

$$\sigma_{allow} = \frac{\sigma_y}{FoS}$$

$\sigma_y$ is the **yield strength**, $FoS$ the **factor of safety**. Typical: 1.5 to 3 for steady loads you know well; much higher for lifting gear and for loads that shock or reverse.

To size a part: area needed = load ÷ allowable stress.
cards.more:
S275 steel yields at 275 MPa. With a factor of safety of 2.5, design to $275 \div 2.5 = 110$ MPa.

A bracket must carry 22 kN. Area needed: $22\,000 \div 110 = 200$ mm². A flat bar 40 × 5 mm is 200 mm²: just enough; pick 40 × 6 for margin.

The factor covers what you do not know: the load could be bigger than quoted, the steel at the low end of its grade, a hole you forgot about. It does not cover fatigue (loads that go up and down millions of times): that has its own rules and much lower allowable stresses.

cards.q: A steel with a yield strength of {sy} MPa is used with a factor of safety of {fs}. What is the allowable stress?
cards.why: The allowable stress is the yield strength shared by the factor of safety.

cards.title: Shear: pins and bolts cut sideways
cards.body:
A pin through a clevis, or a bolt holding two plates that try to slide, is loaded **sideways**: the load tries to cut it. That is **shear stress**, $\tau$ (tau), still load over the area being cut.

- **Single shear**: one cut plane, area $\frac{\pi d^2}{4}$.
- **Double shear**: a pin through a fork (clevis) is cut in **two** places, so twice the area carries the load and the stress halves.

Steels yield in shear at roughly **0.6** of their tensile yield.
cards.more:
Picture scissors: the two blades slide past each other and cut the paper along one line. A bolt through two overlapping plates is the same: one line, single shear.

Now a fork with a pin through both prongs and an eye in the middle. To pull the eye out, the pin must be cut at both sides of it: two lines. That is why clevis pins are so much stronger than they look.

Numbers: a 10 mm pin (78.5 mm²) carries 10 kN. Single shear: $10\,000 \div 78.5 = 127$ MPa. Double shear: $10\,000 \div 157 = 64$ MPa.

cards.q: A {dd} mm clevis pin carries {kn} kN in double shear. What is the shear stress in it?
cards.work: One section: $\frac{\pi \times {dd}^2}{4} = {ar:1}$ mm²; two carry it: $\tau = \frac{{kn} \times 1000}{2 \times {ar:1}} = {answer}$ MPa
cards.why: Double shear: two cross-sections share the load, so divide by twice the area.
cards.hint: How many places must the pin be cut for it to fail?

cards.q: A steel tie rod (E = 200 000 N/mm²) is 16 mm in diameter and 2 m long, and carries 20 kN. How much does it stretch?

steps.ask: The stretch, with L in mm.

cards.why: Area, stress, strain, stretch. Or in one line: $\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AE} = \frac{20\,000 \times 2000}{201 \times 200\,000} = 0.99$ mm. Every length in mm, E in N/mm².

cards.q: Why must L be in millimetres in step 4, and E in N/mm²?
cards.model: Strain has no units, so the stretch comes out in whatever units the length is in: 2000 mm gives mm. And the strain came from stress over E: the stress was in N/mm², so E must be in N/mm² (200 000) for them to divide cleanly. Mixing metres for L with mm for the answer, or GPa for E with MPa for stress, gives an answer out by a factor of 1000.
points: So ΔL has the units of L
Stress and E must be in the same units

cards.q: An aluminium bar (E = 70 000 N/mm²), 25 × 10 mm in section and 1.5 m long, carries 12 kN. How much does it stretch?
cards.why: The same chain. A steel bar the same size would stretch about 0.36 mm: a third as much.

cards.q: A steel bar (E = 200 000 N/mm²) {lm} m long and {ar} mm² in section carries {kn} kN. How much does it stretch?
cards.why: $\Delta L = \frac{FL}{AE}$ with F in N, L in mm, A in mm², E in N/mm².
cards.hint: Newtons and millimetres throughout: kN × 1000, m × 1000.

cards.q: A round tie of S275 steel (yield 275 MPa) must carry {kn} kN with a factor of safety of {fs}. What is the smallest diameter that will do?
cards.why: Allowable stress, then the area that keeps the stress at or under it, then the diameter that gives that area. Round up to the next stock size.
cards.hint: Area needed = load ÷ allowable stress. Then turn $A = \frac{\pi d^2}{4}$ round for d.

cards.q: Checking a 12 mm pin in single shear under 9 kN. One line is wrong. Which?
lines: Allowable shear about 100 MPa, so it is fine
cards.fix: Area: $\frac{\pi \times 12^2}{4} = 113$ mm², so the stress is $9000 \div 113 = 80$ MPa: closer to the limit than it looked
cards.why: $\pi d^2$ without the ÷ 4 makes the area four times too big and the stress four times too small. Check: a 12 mm pin is a bit over 100 mm² (a 10 mm one is about 79).

cards.q: Why is a ductile steel bracket safer than a cast iron one of the same strength, if it is overloaded?
options: It bends visibly before it breaks
It is always stronger in tension
It cannot yield under any load
It weighs less for the same strength
cards.why: Ductile metal yields and stretches a long way before fracture: the bracket sags, which someone can see. Brittle cast iron breaks with almost no warning.

cards.q: A {lm} m bar stretches by {dl} mm under load. What is the strain, in microstrain?
cards.why: Strain is stretch ÷ length, both in mm; × 1 000 000 for microstrain.
cards.hint: Length in mm first, so both are in the same units.

cards.q: A hydraulic cylinder's piston rod is {dd} mm in diameter and pushes with {kn} kN. What is the compressive stress in the rod, in MPa?
cards.why: Compression works the same way as tension: load over area. (Long thin rods can also buckle at a lower load: that is a separate check.)
cards.hint: Area of the rod from its diameter, then load over area.

cards.q: A pipe wall carries a stress of {mp} MPa. What is that in bar?
cards.why: 1 MPa = 1 N/mm² = 10 bar. Stress and pressure are both force per area, so the same units fit both.

cards.q: A 10 mm bolt holds two overlapping plates that are pulled apart along their length. The bolt is loaded in…
cards.why: The plates try to slide past each other, cutting the bolt across where they meet: one plane, single shear. A bolt is in tension when the load pulls along its axis, as in a hanging bracket.

cards.q: A rod is replaced with one of twice the diameter, same material and load. The stress becomes…
cards.why: Area goes with diameter squared: twice the diameter, four times the area, a quarter of the stress. Twice the area (not diameter) would halve it.

cards.q: A bar carries a load. You swap it for one with three times the area. The stress is…
cards.why: Stress = load ÷ area: three times the area, a third of the stress.

cards.q: A {dd} mm round bar carries {kn} kN in tension. What is the stress?
cards.why: Load in N over the area $\frac{\pi d^2}{4}$.

cards.q: A steel rod (E = 200 000 N/mm²), {lm} m long, carries a stress of {mp} MPa. How much does it stretch?
cards.why: Strain = stress ÷ E; stretch = strain × length (in mm).

cards.q: Match each term with its meaning.
